Chadron|United States of America.f: When the railroad bypassed the first townsite, residents moved the whole town, buildings and all, six miles to Chadron.

Mineral Wells|United States of America.f: Nearly every US helicopter pilot who flew in Vietnam trained at Fort Wolters, right outside Mineral Wells.

North Bend|United States of America.f: Louis Simpson merged the town of Yarrow with his father's sawmill site in 1903 and renamed the result North Bend.

Page|United States of America.f: Page began as Government Camp for Glen Canyon Dam workers, then took the name of Reclamation commissioner John C. Page.

McGrath|United States of America.f: McGrath became a regional supply hub as the northernmost point on the Kuskokwim River reachable by large riverboats.

Merced|United States of America.f: UC Merced, opened here in 2005, was the first research university built in the United States in the 21st century.

Unalakleet|United States of America.f: In 1898 the US brought Sami reindeer herders from Lapland to Unalakleet to teach herding to local people.

Salem|United States of America.f: The Kalapuya people called the site Chim-i-ki-ti, thought to mean meeting or resting place, long before it became Salem.

Sidney|United States of America.f: Sidney was named by a justice of the peace after Sidney Walters, a six-year-old boy staying at his house.

Glendive|United States of America.f: Irish sportsman Sir George Gore named the local creek Glendive in 1855 on a hunt that killed 105 bears and 2,000 buffalo.

Port Clinton|United States of America.f: Port Clinton calls itself the Walleye Capital of the World and drops a giant walleye every New Year's Eve.

Massena|United States of America.f: Massena had a pair of sulfur springs, one hot and one cold, that drew resort hotels from the 1820s.

New Haven|United States of America.f: New Haven was laid out in 1639 as a three-by-three grid called the Nine Square Plan, one of the first planned US cities.

Egegik|United States of America.f: Egegik had 39 residents in 2020 but 243 housing units, about 90 percent of them vacant.

Salmon|United States of America.f: Sacagawea, the Lewis and Clark guide, was born in the Lemhi Valley near Salmon.

Taos|United States of America.f: Taos Pueblo, next to the town, has been occupied for nearly a thousand years and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Dubois|United States of America.f: The town was first named for founder John Rumbarger, then renamed for local lumber magnate John DuBois.

Olympia|United States of America.f: Olympia's music scene helped drive 1990s punk movements such as riot grrrl and grunge.

Lebanon|United States of America.f: Lebanon is home to Dartmouth-Hitchcock, the largest medical facility between Boston and Burlington, Vermont.

Altoona|United States of America.f: One theory says a railroad engineer named Altoona after Altona, a German railway town now part of Hamburg.

Hyannis|United States of America.f: Hyannis is named after Iyannough, a sachem of the Cummaquid band of the Wampanoag.

Rockland|United States of America.f: By 1854 Rockland had 12 lime quarries and 125 kilns, making it the leading lime producer in the United States.

New Bedford|United States of America.f: At the peak of its whaling boom in the 1800s, New Bedford was the wealthiest city in North America per capita.

Arlington|United States of America.f: Arlington's airport was built by Depression-era relief projects and later served as a naval air station in World War II.

Imperial|United States of America.f: Imperial, plotted in 1902 by the Imperial Land Company, was the first city in its valley to incorporate, in 1904.

Rutland|United States of America.f: Rutland grew into one of the world's leading marble producers, drawing Italian quarry workers after the railroad arrived in 1851.

Havre|United States of America.f: Havre was renamed after Le Havre in France, and the first town meeting to pick the name ended in a brawl.

Bar Harbor|United States of America.f: In 1604 Champlain ran aground off here and named the island Isles des Monts Deserts, meaning island of barren mountains.

Morgantown|United States of America.f: Morgantown runs a Personal Rapid Transit system, one of the few automated people movers in the United States.

Waimea|United States of America.f: Waimea's post office is named Kamuela because a state cannot have two post offices with the same name and Kauai has a Waimea.

Northway|United States of America.f: The highest sea-level pressure ever recorded in the US, 31.85 inches, was measured at Northway on January 31, 1989.

Wolf Point|United States of America.f: Wolf Point hosts the Wadopana Pow-wow, billed as the oldest traditional pow wow in Montana, and a Wild Horse Stampede.

Iliamna|United States of America.f: Residents of Old Iliamna moved the village about 35 miles west to its present site in 1935.

Augusta (ME)|United States of America.f: Augusta is the easternmost state capital in the United States.

Crescent City|United States of America.f: In 1964 four tsunami waves from the Great Alaskan earthquake destroyed much of Crescent City.

Glasgow (MT)|United States of America.f: Glasgow was named when a railroader spun a globe and his finger landed on Glasgow, Scotland.

Destin|United States of America.f: Destin sits on a former barrier island that technically became an island again when the Choctawhatchee-West Bay Canal opened in the 1940s.

Gulkana|United States of America.f: The Gulkana River runs 60 miles to the Copper River, with the Trans-Alaska Pipeline following alongside.

Lanai City|United States of America.f: James Dole built Lanai City in the 1920s to house his pineapple workers, creating the first model city in Hawaii.

Hilton Head Island|United States of Amer.f: The island is named for Captain William Hilton, who in 1663 spotted a headland that mapmakers called Hilton's Headland.
